finding.claim: deleteAccount calls canDelete() but discards the boolean result, so no authorization is enforced. Any user can delete any account by id. The sibling closeAccount correctly uses assertCanDelete(), which throws.
finding.source: Any authenticated user calling DELETE /accounts/{id} with an arbitrary account id (the id path parameter and the caller's User are attacker-controlled).
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at line 23 — deletion of an account that the caller neither owns nor administers.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) is the DELETE /accounts/{id} handler; id comes from the request
Account looked up by attacker-supplied id with no ownership check
canDelete(u, a) returns false for non-owner non-admin, but the return value is ignored, so execution continues
accounts.remove(id) executes unconditionally, giving an IDOR/broken access control

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (lines 9-11) is a correct predicate, but its result is unused in deleteAccount. There is no assertCanDelete call, no exception, and no other check on this path. Compare closeAccount (line 29), which enforces the check. No authentication or authorization is visible at the controller or framework level in this single-file codebase. If the account id does not exist, a.ownerId() would throw a NullPointerException, but that does not block deletion of existing accounts.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) is a bool predicate whose result is discarded at line 22; assertCanDelete (13-17) throws but is only used in closeAccount (line 29). No other guard in the single-file codebase.
verdict.reason: src/AccountService.java:22 calls canDelete(u, a) as a bare statement, discarding the boolean, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any caller, unlike closeAccount which uses the throwing assertCanDelete at line 29.
